t: before the sun rises, from when the face of the entire east lights up. The time when the light is noticeable in the east, after the sun begins to light up and before the sun's disk has risen (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yoma 3:1).

and once the hour pressed... and they offered the morning tamid at the fourth hour of the day. Although the preferred time for offering it is right in the morning, its time extends to a third of the day, the end of four 'seasonal hours' from the start of the day (whose length varies according to the length of the day). And in an emergency they offer until this time.

once the shadow lengthens and it is noticeable to all that it has lengthened. In the middle of the day the sun is in the middle of the sky and the shadow is short. After the sun begins to incline toward the west the shadow becomes long, and when it is noticeable that the shadow has lengthened, the time for slaughtering the tamid begins.
from six and a half hours and onward until the end of the day. From half a seasonal hour after midday until sunset.
every day. Ordinarily (except for the eve of Pesach, as below halakhah 5; and see also Hilchot Tefillah 3:2).
because of the offerings of individuals or of the community. Which must be offered that same day.

because it is forbidden to offer any sacrifice before the morning tamid, and one does not slaughter an offering after the afternoon tamid. Therefore the afternoon tamid must be delayed so that there will be enough time to offer the sacrifices.

except for the Pesach offering alone, since it is impossible for all of Israel to offer their Pesach offerings in two hours. The slaughter of the tamid is done every day at eight and a half hours, except on the day of the Pesach offering, when they would advance the slaughter of the tamid (below halakhah 5), since the Pesach offering is offered on the fourteenth of Nisan after the tamid offering (Hilchot Korban Pesach 1:4), and more than two hours are needed for all of Israel to manage to slaughter and offer the sacrifice (Har HaMoriah, Even HaAzel).
the Pesach offering is slaughtered only after the afternoon tamid. See also Hilchot Korban Pesach 1:4.

those lacking atonement. Zavim, zavot, women after childbirth and metzora'im who have become pure of their impurity and have not yet brought the offering that completes their purification process, and are forbidden to eat sacrificial food (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:1).

they offer their atonement after the afternoon tamid, etc.. Ideally they should bring their offering before the tamid. However, if they did not offer it, they were permitted to transgress the prohibition of offering after the tamid so that they could offer and eat the Pesach offering, which is a positive commandment whose neglect is punishable by karet (Bavli Pesachim 59a; see also Hilchot Korban Pesach 6:4).

so that they will have time to roast before Shabbat enters. The Pesach offering must be roasted after it is offered, and it can also be roasted at night before it is eaten. However, when the fourteenth of Nisan falls on Friday, its roasting must be completed before Shabbat, and therefore they would then advance the offering of the tamid.

they burn anything fit for burning all day. For example, the handful and the frankincense, which by law may be offered all day until evening (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 4:4, following Aruch HaShulchan 101:16).
as we have explained in Ma'aseh HaKorbanot. 4:2.
and limbs and fats that were not consumed. That were burned on the altar and were not properly consumed.
they turn them over. To hasten their burning.

the limbs of the tamid override impurity. Burning the limbs is permitted in impurity when it is impossible to burn them in purity, like communal offerings with a set time (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 4:10).
but they do not override Shabbat. One may not burn on Shabbat the limbs of the Friday tamid (but the limbs of the Shabbat tamid are burned on Shabbat, Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 4:3).

for the tamid, its beginning overrides Shabbat and its end does not override. When its performance begins on Shabbat (the Shabbat tamid), it overrides Shabbat in all its acts (including burning), and when only its end falls on Shabbat (the Friday tamid whose limbs were not burned), it does not override Shabbat.
the fats of Shabbat are offered on Yom Tov nights. It is permitted to offer them.

as it is stated, 'the burnt offering of Shabbat on its Shabbat,' and not on another Shabbat. This includes the burnt offering of Yom Kippur, which is called 'Shabbat.' On the other hand, from this verse we learn that the Shabbat burnt offering is offered on Yom Tov (see Bavli Shabbat 114a).

and not a weekday burnt offering on Yom Tov. This is another law learned from this verse, that only the Shabbat burnt offering is offered on Yom Tov ('on its Shabbat'), but a weekday burnt offering is not offered on Yom Tov (see Bavli Shabbat 24b).
because they are like the fats of Shabbat. But if it falls on a weekday, the fats are not burned on Yom Tov (Hilchot Korban Pesach 1:8).
the examined ones. Checked, without blemish.
in the Lamb Chamber in the Temple. One of the four chambers in the Beit HaMoked (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:10).
and they should be prepared four days before the day of their offering. And on the fifth day they would offer them (Commentary on the Mishnah, Arakhin 2:5).
and they give it water to drink... so that it is easy to flay. So that the skin will not stick to the flesh.
like the procedure of the burnt offering that we wrote in Ma'aseh HaKorbanot. Chapter 6.
and they did not bind the lamb. Tying its legs and arms together.
lest they imitate the heretics. For they would do so in slaughtering their sacrifices to idolatry (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tamid 4:1).

rather they held its hands and feet in their hands, and this was its binding. Holding the lamb at the time of slaughter ('its binding') was done by gripping its front and hind legs in their hands (although after Yochanan the High Priest installed rings at the slaughtering place in the Temple courtyard, they would catch the animal's legs with the rings, Commentary on the Mishnah, Tamid 4:1; and see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:14).

at the northwest corner of the slaughterhouse, at the second ring, etc.. In the north of the altar there were twenty-four rings, and there they would slaughter the sacrificial animals (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:14). The tamid was slaughtered on the north side of the rings: in the morning at the western ring in the second row, and in the afternoon at the eastern ring in the second row (for the reason for slaughtering in the second row see Tiferet Yisrael, Tamid 4:1).
so that it would be opposite the sun. Facing the sun, which shines from the east in the morning and from the west in the afternoon.
words of tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
that the altar of the burnt offering is inaugurated only with the morning tamid. For the manner of inaugurating the golden altar, the menorah and the table see below 3:1, 3:11, 5:3.
a fire kept burning. Lit.

and although the fire comes down from heaven, it is a mitzvah to bring fire from a commoner. Although there is fire on the altar that came down from heaven miraculously, as in the days of Moses and Solomon (Leviticus 9:24, II Chronicles 7:1; and see Bavli Zevachim 61b), and wood is not needed to sustain this fire, one is obligated to add wood.
a pile. An arranged stack of wood.
a large pile of fire. For offering the tamid and the other sacrifices (below halakhah 4).
logs of wood. Their length and width were one cubit (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 7:3).
in addition to the wood of the pile. After they arranged the wood of the large pile, they would bring up two more logs to increase the fire (below 6:1).
they make three fire piles on the top of the altar each day. And on Yom Kippur they would add another pile (see Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 2:5).
from which they take fire in the pan to burn incense every day. From this pile they took coals for burning the incense (see below 3:5).
for the fulfillment of the mitzvah of the fire. They did not use it for anything; it burned specifically for the mitzvah of keeping fire burning on the altar (above, halakhah 1).

but limbs and fats that were not consumed from the evening, etc.. When clearing last night's ashes of the pile, they leave the limbs and fats that were not burned during the night at the side of the altar (below halakhah 13), and after arranging the pile they burn them again beside the pile (the center of the pile was left for the limbs of the tamid and the sacrifices of that day, Rikuv).

pan fire and menorah fire, etc.. From the altar they took fire in a pan for burning incense (below 3:5) and fire for lighting the menorah (below 3:13). Fire taken out from the pile for this, even if it is still on the altar, is not considered altar fire, and one who extinguishes it is exempt.
it was removed for another mitzvah. The status of the fire changed and it was transferred to be designated for another mitzvah.

and its appearance should be that he began arranging from the east. He should make a mark in the arrangement of the wood on the east so that it appears that he began arranging from there (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tamid 2:4).

and there was a gap between the logs. From which they would ignite the coals of the second pile for incense (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.; and according to the Rosh and the commentator there, in these gaps they would insert thin pieces of wood from which the wood of the pile was kindled, compare Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 3:9).

on the ashes in the middle of the altar, which is called the tapuach. The ashes of the pile were cleared to a heap in the middle of the altar (below halakhah 13), called the tapuach (apple) after its appearance (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tamid 2:2).
good fig wood. Other woods are also valid, but they were accustomed to these (see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 7:3).
and in it about five se'ah of coals. An amount of wood whose burning would produce five se'ah of coals (an amount sufficient for the incense).

because on it they burn every Shabbat the two bowls of frankincense of the showbread. Besides the coals taken from it for the incense, on this pile on Shabbat they burned the bowls of frankincense that were on the showbread table (below 5:2-5).
the removal of the ashes from the altar. Taking the ashes out from it.
and it is one of the priestly services. See also Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 9:8.
lesser than the garments used for the other services. Less honorable, since they become soiled with ashes.

because it is not proper to pour a cup for his master in the clothes in which he cooked a pot for his master. And therefore it is not fitting to serve in the Temple services in garments soiled with the ashes of the pile.
when do they remove the ashes?. The removal of the ashes is valid from the night (Bavli Yoma 20b), and the exact time was set according to need.
from when the dawn column rises. The beginning of lighting in the east before sunrise (about an hour and a fifth before it, Commentary on the Mishnah, Berakhot 1:1).

and on festivals from the last third of the night. On festivals there were many ashes that had to be cleared from the pile to the tapuach after the removal of the ashes (as below halakhah 13), and therefore they had to start earlier (Rashi, Yoma 20b).
and on Yom Kippur from midnight. So that the High Priest could begin the day's services right in the morning before he grows weak (Tosafot there in the name of Ri).
the one who merited to remove. In the lottery held among the priests (below 4:5).
and he puts on the garments of removal. Above, halakhah 10.
and sanctifies his hands and feet. From the laver, as every priest does when beginning to serve (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 5:1).

and they say to him, 'Be careful not to touch the vessel until you have sanctified your hands and feet'. Since this is the first service of the day, the priest has not yet sanctified his hands and feet (Rikuv, and see there further reasons why this was said specifically to the priest who removes the ashes).
the pan. A shovel for collecting the coals.
in the corner. In the corner.
and scoops from the coals that were consumed in the heart of the fire. He gathers into the pan the coals that were well burned from the middle of the pile.
and turns his face to the north. When he reaches the floor after descending the ramp toward the south.
in the place where they put the crop of the bird. There they throw the crop of the bird burnt offering (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 6:21).
and the clearing of the inner altar and the menorah. The charcoal and ashes that remained on the incense altar, and the used wicks with the remains of the menorah's oil (below 3:12).
the shovels. Scoops for sweeping the ashes.
the forks. Spits for removing limbs.
and if the sides cannot hold. If there is not enough room on the sides of the altar.
they return them to the sides of the altar. And after arranging the new pile they would return them to the fire (above, halakhah 5).
they arrange them on the ramp opposite the sovev. They place them on the ramp at the height of the sovev.
on the tapuach. In the middle of the altar.
a letech. Fifteen se'ah, about one hundred twenty-five liters.
because it is an ornament for the altar. So that it will be seen that many sacrifices were offered. [Note: Rambam writes and vocalizes the word 'noy' in the Commentary on the Mishnah as 'no'i'.]
to the place where the ashes are poured. The place where sin offerings that are burned outside Jerusalem are burned (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:4).
and never did a priest become lazy about taking out the ashes. Although it is not a service.
blemished ones. Blemished priests who are disqualified from Temple service and forbidden to enter from the altar inward (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 6:1).
the streams. Streams of water.
and it is forbidden to benefit from it. See also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:13.
and the afternoon. Above 1:3.
the weight of a hundred dinars. About four hundred eighty grams.
an altar that was uprooted. Moved from its place.
they burn incense in its place. In the place where the altar should be.
even kerat. Pieces (and not only powder, and see Radbaz).
and likewise at the time he enters with the blood of the sin offerings performed inside. To sprinkle the blood of the inner sin offerings (see also Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 4:2).
as it is stated, 'and no person, etc.'. It is said regarding the High Priest's entry for burning incense and sprinkling the blood of the sin offerings on Yom Kippur.
a binyan av. A halakhic source that forms the basis for other laws learned from it.
atonement within the sanctuary. In the Heikhal.
the one who merited the clearing of the inner altar. In the lottery held among the priests as to who would perform the various services (below 4:6).
enters. The Heikhal.
two and a half kavs. About three and a half liters.
the ashes and charcoal that are in the altar. In the golden altar, from yesterday's incense.
and finally he sweeps the rest into it. When only a little ash remained, he would sweep it from the altar into the vessel.
and puts the bowl in another vessel, whose name was kaf. So that the incense not be scattered on the floor (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tamid 5:4).
and with him another. The priest who merited the pan (see next halakhah).
with a pan of fire in his hand. A shovel full of burning coals.
the one who merited the pan. The priest who merited the removal of the ashes also merited this (below 4:5).
the coals that were consumed in the second pile. The coals that were well burned in the second fire pile on the altar, which was for taking fire for the incense (above 2:4).
and descends and pours them into a golden pan. And he did not scoop with the golden pan so as not to lose Israel's money (Bavli Yoma 44b).

if some of the coals scattered, about a kav or less, etc.. The silver pan held four kavs and the golden pan held three kavs (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tamid 5:5), and therefore the coals were scattered. If more than a kav of coals scattered, the golden pan was not filled and he had to scoop again (Rikuv).
he sweeps them into the channel. The water channel in the Temple.
the pesachter. A large vessel (above 2:13).
and for the creeping creature on Shabbat. That was found dead in the courtyard (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:20).
and they bring down with it the ashes from the altar. Above 2:13.
and he goes before them. He enters the Heikhal before the priests with the incense and the pan.
and takes the teni, in which was the clearings of the altar. And he throws the ashes in the ash room east of the ramp (below halakhah 12).
and prostrates and exits. As is done at the end of every service performed in the Heikhal (see also below halakhot 9 and 17).
and he spreads them. Flattens them over the altar.
and the one in whose hand is the kaf. The priest who burns the incense.
and gives it to his beloved or his relative. Those whom he chose to enter with him into the Heikhal for this purpose.

and sees if some of the incense scattered a little in the kaf, etc.. The beloved or relative would put into the cupped hands of the priest burning the incense the incense from the bowl and the incense that scattered in the kaf.

and they say to this one who burns. Burning the incense was generally done by a priest who had never burned it before (below 4:7-8), and therefore he had to be warned (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tamid 6:3).

be careful not to begin in front of you, lest you be burned. That he not begin scattering the incense on the side of the altar near him but on the side far from him, so he not be burned by the smoke of the burning incense.
like one who sifts fine flour until it spreads, etc.. He spreads and flattens the incense over the whole fire.
and if he is a High Priest. The High Priest may perform any service he wishes, even without a lottery (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 5:12).
clearing the menorah and trimming its lamps. Cleaning it of waste and lighting the lamps, below halakhah 12.
overrides Shabbat and impurity like offerings that have a fixed time. Shabbat is desecrated for it and it is done in impurity when it is impossible to do it in purity (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 4:9).
half a log. About one hundred seventy cc.
and cleans it. Wipes the lamp of remains of oil.
in the place of the ashes next to the altar. East of the ramp (above 2:12).
and lights a lamp that went out. After clearing the extinguished lamps and renewing the oil and wick in them, he would light them.
and a lamp he found that had not gone out, he fixes it. He adds oil to it without extinguishing it.
the western lamp. The middle lamp whose wick faced west (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 3:8).
from the outer altar. By fire brought from the altar.
because the lamps are fixed in the menorah. And it is impossible to detach them and light with them (see also Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 3:6).
and he cannot light it from another lamp. To light an external lamp from one of the lamps of the menorah and with it light the other lamp.
for it is forbidden to light with them in the menorah on Shabbat. Wicks that the fire does not take well in, and it is forbidden to light Shabbat lamps with them (Hilchot Shabbat 5:5).
so that a flame rises on its own. So that the fire takes hold of the wick well upon lighting and they will not need to fix it later.
and they perform another service. Burning the incense (below 6:4, and see Piskei u-Shitot there).
to make the whole courtyard aware. To publicize the service through the double entry.
and afterward. After they interrupted with another service (above halakhah 15).
any lamp that went out, they light it from one of them as we have explained. Above halakhah 13.
the one who merited the clearing of the menorah. Below 4:6.
resembling a large kiton. It looked like a large liquid container.
he clears into it. He removes into it.
on the second step of the three steps before it. Next to the menorah were three steps on which the priest stands when he clears and lights the menorah (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 3:11).
the High Priest's chavitin. A meal offering made in a pan (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 13:2-4), and every day it was offered on behalf of the High Priest.
and their kneading and baking override Shabbat. Not only does their offering override Shabbat but also their kneading and baking, which cannot be done on Friday.

and impurity. When the priests or the vessels became impure (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 4:12). But when the High Priest becomes impure, a substitute is appointed for him and he offers it (below halakhah 20).
'baked' so that it be fine. And what was baked yesterday is not fine.

it becomes disqualified by lodging, since the pan is one of the sacred vessels. Something sanctified in a sacred vessel and through which a night has passed is disqualified (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 3:18).
for the pan is one of the sacred vessels as we have explained. The vessel in which the meal offering is fried was a service vessel (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 12:23).
grinding their fine flour and sifting them outside. Unlike their kneading and baking (ibid.).
and they do not override Shabbat. For they can be done on Friday.
and they appointed another priest. After they offered half of the first one's meal offering in the morning.
that their form would pass. They would become moldy and spoil.
and likewise if the half of the afternoon was lost or became impure. They bring a whole isaron and offer half of it and burn half.
and where do they burn them? In the courtyard. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:3.
and it was offered whole. When the meal offering was not brought by a High Priest, they did not divide it and offer half; rather they offered all of it.

the High Priest died before they offered in the morning... they offer it. His heirs, on the day he died (but on the following days until another priest is appointed, they offer it from the Temple chamber's funds and the obligation falls on the community - Or Sameach, Likkutei Halakhot, Menachot 51b based on Hilchot Shekalim 4:4; and see Lechem Mishneh).

rather, they set aside for them three logs of oil and a handful of frankincense. This is the amount of oil and frankincense offered with the High Priest's isaron when it is divided (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 13:2).
they would do them by lottery. The determination of which priest would perform which service was done by lot.
the priests of the ancestral house of the day. The priests serving in the Temple that day.

to the Chamber of Hewn Stone. Which was in the north of the courtyard, half in the sacred area and half in the non-sacred area (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:17). The lotteries were conducted in its sacred half (Bavli Yoma 25a).
and the one appointed over the lotteries. He was one of the fifteen officers who were in the Temple (see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 7:8).
in a circle. In a ring.
he takes the turban off the head of one of them and puts it back. To mark that from this man they begin counting (below halakhah 3).
and they cast lots as will be explained. Below halakhah 3.
and the men who serve go out to the service. The priests who won the lottery go to serve.
they deliver them to the attendants. They transfer the priests to the authority of the attendants who assist the one in charge of the priestly garments (Tiferet Yisrael, Tamid 5:3).
and they did not leave on them anything but the trousers alone. For reasons of modesty.
and the attendants return the garments to the windows. In which the priestly garments are stored (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 8:8).
one or two. Each priest would extend one finger or two, and the officer counted the extended fingers.

and one does not extend a thumb in the Temple, because of the deceivers, etc.. So that they not raise or bend the thumb if they see that the count is about to end, so that the lot falls to them (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yoma 2:1, Responsa of Rambam 126).
and one who extends a thumb, it is not counted for him. The thumb, rather the other fingers (Rikuv).

he is the one who came out first in the lottery for the service. He is the first winner, and in lotteries in which several winners won (below halakhah 7), those who stand after him win the other roles.
because it is forbidden to count Israel except by means of something else. That each one bring some item (object) and they count the items, and thus the number of people is known.
and he counted them with the lambs. When King Saul counted his fighters, he did not count them directly but by means of lambs.
who clears the altar. Removes ashes from the altar (above 2:10).
arranges the pile. Arranges wood for the fire pile on the altar.
brings up two logs of wood to the altar. Which were added to the fire pile every day (ibid. halakhah 2).
brings in a pan full of fire from the outer altar, etc.. Above 3:5.
and counts as we have explained. Above halakhah 3.

the fifth brings up the head of the tamid and its leg to the ramp, etc.. The order of bringing the limbs up to the ramp is fixed for all communal offerings (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 6:11-16; for a description of the slaughter of the tamid and bringing it up to the altar see below 6:1-5).
the head of the tamid and its leg. The right hind leg.
the two arms. The front legs.
the rump and the leg. The rear part of the animal: the end of the spine and the tail, and the left hind leg (ibid. halakhah 9).
and the breast. The neck.
the two flanks. The flesh and ribs on both sides of the animal.
the innards. The intestines and the other organs of the digestive system.
fine flour of the libations... the wine of the libations. Which they would bring with burnt offerings and peace offerings (ibid. 2:1).
the chavitin. The chavitin meal offering of the High Priest (above 3:18).

one who never burned incense in his life may come and cast lots. For the priests would say that one who burns incense becomes wealthy, and many priests wanted to merit its burning, so they included in the lottery only priests who had not burned it before (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yoma 2:3).
and the additional offerings. On Shabbat they offered two lambs in addition to the tamid lambs.
and the two bowls of frankincense. Two vessels full of frankincense that were placed all week on the table beside the showbread and which are burned on the altar on Shabbat (below halakhah 11).

the people of that ancestral house of the outgoing watch. On Shabbat the watches of the priests who worked in the Temple for a week changed, and the services were divided between the finishing watch and the beginning watch.
and the frankincense requires salt like the other sacrifices. Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:11.
and two priests offer the two bowls. The priests of the incoming watch (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tamid 6:3).

the incoming ones divide among themselves in the north. The north of the courtyard, where the slaughter of the most holy sacrifices was done (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:2), and those who divide on this side show that the service of the incoming week belongs to them.
on the Shabbat that is within the festival. During Chol HaMoed.

all the watches divide equally in the showbread. For on the festivals all the watches take part in the festival sacrifices, in dividing their meat and hides and in dividing the showbread (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:4-6).
because they were early to the service. Only on Yom Tov does the service fall to all the watches, and the priests who come early receive from the showbread as payment for their earliness.

so that the priests will stay late for the sake of the division of the showbread. Because of the distribution of the bread, the priests will remain for service on the Shabbat adjacent to the festival even though they are not of the weekly watch and this Shabbat is not part of the festival.

and if one of the members of the watch was late and did not come, another will be found. Since many priests of the other watches will remain, no lack will be felt if some of the priests of the incoming watch come only after Shabbat.

that the first day of the festival fell on Monday. The watch entering service in the week of the festival would have only the first day to work without the other watches (since on Shabbat the outgoing watch shares the work with it and on Yom Tov all the watches take part in the service), and many members of the watch would be lazy to come.
the last day of Yom Tov on Thursday. The watch that served in the week of the festival would have only Friday to work without the other watches, and many were lazy to come.
a watch whose time is fixed in that Shabbat. That works a whole week.

and this incoming one. The watch that works only the day before or after Yom Tov (and in the case where the last day of Yom Tov falls on Thursday the law is reversed, and the incoming watch that works a whole week will take ten loaves).

the High Priest always takes half of the loaves from every watch. He is not required to take them, but only if he wishes (see Tosefta Kifshuta, Sukkah p. 906). And from the other sacrifices the priest may take as much as he wishes (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:18).
and the High Priest does not take a pras. A divided loaf.
and it is a clear matter in the Torah that it is twelve loaves. As is written there at the beginning of the passage: 'You shall take fine flour and bake it into twelve loaves' (Leviticus 24:5).
two rows. Arranged stacks of bread.
three golden tubes. Each in the shape of a hollow half-reed (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 3:14). And between the upper bread and the bread beneath it there were only two tubes (ibid. halakhah 15).
so that the wind may blow through it. Through the bread, by means of the gap that would form between the loaves.
and he supports each pile with two forks. Split Y-shaped posts on which they propped the piles of bread (ibid. halakhah 13).
and they place beside each pile a vessel containing a handful of frankincense. On the table in the gap between the two piles.
and the bowls had bases. A flat bottom, so that they could stand without leaning on the bread (unlike the blood basins, which had no bases, see Hilchot Korban Pesach 1:13).
the rows hold each other back, etc.. One does not fulfill the obligation by placing one row, or one bowl, or loaves without bowls or bowls without loaves.
from Shabbat to Shabbat. Every Shabbat.
for the two watches, the incoming and the outgoing, divide with the High Priest. As explained above 4:12-14.

two with two rows in their hands. Without the tubes between them. And below, halakhah 11, it is explained that on Friday they would remove the tubes from the rows and at the end of Shabbat they would put them in between the loaves.
they enter. The Heikhal.
these pull. The priests standing in the south pull the bread out toward themselves.
and these place. Those standing in the north.

and the handbreadth of this one into the handbreadth of that one. As they pulled out the bread they would place the new bread on the table, so that opposite each handbreadth of loaves coming out they would place a handbreadth of loaves going in.
before Me always. So that the table never be without bread, even for a short time.

and they put the bread they took out on another golden table that was in the Ulam. In the Ulam there were two tables: a marble one on which they placed the bread from the time of baking until Shabbat, and a second golden one on which they placed the bread on Shabbat until its distribution (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 3:16).
and they burned the bowls. They burned the frankincense in the bowls on the altar.
and if Yom Kippur fell on Shabbat. And it is forbidden then to eat the loaves.
twenty-four se'ah of wheat. About 180 liters.
wheat fit for meal offerings. See Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 6:11-13, 7:4.
and they rub them and tread on them like the other wheat of meal offerings. Rubbing the wheat by hand three hundred times and treading on it with the foot five hundred times (ibid. 7:4-5).

and they sift from them with eleven sieves. The grains of fine flour are the coarse grains from grinding wheat (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 6:11-12) that remain in the sieve, and the flour (the fine part resembling dust) falls through.
twenty-four isaron of fine flour. About 60 liters; it turns out that after sifting a third of the amount of wheat originally brought remains.
or if he did not take them out of twenty-four se'ah. See also below 8:5.
their kneading and shaping outside. Like the Two Loaves (below 8:7).
and their baking inside in the courtyard like the other meal offerings. And in them the kneading too was done inside (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 12:21).
molds. Forms.
in which they put the loaf, which is dough. To shape its form.
it would break. It would be broken.
that it have many faces. Six sides (top, bottom and four directions).
and its height. Its thickness.
and there remains between the two ends, etc.. After they folded the ends of the loaf from both sides, a gap remains between the two folded ends of the loaf.
and they arrange them the next day. On the golden table.
and neither arranging the tubes nor removing them overrides Shabbat. Placing the golden tubes between the new loaves and removing them from the old ones (above halakhah 2) is not done on Shabbat.
and he places them along the length of the table. On the floor next to the length of the table (Tosafot, Menachot 96a).
and on the first day of the week he enters. At the end of Shabbat, the night leading to Sunday (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 11:6, Har HaMoriah).

he arranged the bread on Shabbat as required and did not place with it bowls of frankincense until the next day... the bread is disqualified and not sanctified. It is forbidden to eat the bread, and it is not even sanctified to the extent that it be considered sacrificial food that was disqualified (see below halakhah 14).

and likewise if he arranged the bread and bowls on Sunday... the bread is not sanctified and is disqualified. Since the bread and bowls were not placed on Shabbat and the bowls were not burned on Shabbat, the bread is not sanctified.

but if he burned the bowls on Shabbat, the bread is disqualified. And is sanctified, since the bowls were burned on Shabbat (and unlike the first clause, where it is not sanctified even though the bowls were burned on Shabbat, since the bread and bowls were not placed together - see Rikuv, and see Radbaz, Kesef Mishneh and other commentators who found Rambam's words difficult and explained and even emended them in various ways).

what should he do with bread and bowls he arranged after Shabbat, etc.. And it helps only in the case where he arranged the bread and bowls after Shabbat and not in the case where he arranged the bread on Shabbat and the bowls after Shabbat (see Radbaz).

he should leave them there on the table until the day of Shabbat passes over them while they are arranged. And in this way it turns out that the bread and bowls were on the table for a week from Shabbat to Shabbat.

for even if the bread remained with the bowls on the table for several Shabbatot, there is nothing in that. For as long as the bread and bowls are on the table they are valid and are not disqualified by lodging (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 11:8).

the bread is disqualified and is like sacrifices that were disqualified. Since the bread and bowls were arranged properly on Shabbat the bread is sanctified, but since the bowls were burned out of their time the bread was disqualified.

for which they are liable... as will be explained. One who eats sacrificial food that was disqualified through piggul or notar, and likewise an impure person who ate sacrificial food, are liable to karet (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 18, halakhot 6, 10, 13).
a loaf was broken. Was broken.

if before he removed the bread from the table, etc.. The law of the bread and bowls in this case is similar to a meal offering that became deficient before the handful was taken, which is not burned (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 11:16).

and if after he removed the bread the bread was broken, it is disqualified and he burns the bowls on it. In this case the bowls are considered the handful of the meal offering and the bread the remainder of the offering, and when the remainder of a meal offering became deficient after the handful was taken, the handful is burned (ibid. halakhah 20, and see also ibid. 12:4).

the impure in his impurity and the pure in his purity. They eat the pure bread and do not eat the impure. And if one of the bowls became impure, they burn both (for offering in impurity is permitted for the community but eating in impurity is forbidden even for the community, Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 4:9-11), burning the impure one in impurity and the pure one in purity (Tosefta Menachot 3:2 and Bavli there 15a).
close to the rising of dawn, etc.. See also Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 8:11.
and he knocks on the courtyard and they open for him. The officer knocks on the gates of the Beit HaMoked and the elder priests there open for him (ibid.).
and they search the entire courtyard. To see that everything is in its place (Rav Ovadiah of Bartenura, Tamid 1:3), or to see that there is no impurity there (Rikuv).
and they appoint the makers of the chavitin to make the chavitin. The chavitin meal offering of the High Priest.
and all the priests who are there... and each one merits his task as we explained. Above 4:1-6.
and he removes the ashes in the order we explained. Above 2:12.
and afterward he arranges the pile, etc.. Above 2:2-4.
to the Chamber of Vessels. Where the Temple vessels were stored.
and they give the tamid water to drink. Above 1:9.
to the slaughterhouse. There they slaughtered the tamid (above 1:11).

until they open the gate of the great Heikhal. They would enter the Heikhal through the northern wicket (a small gate beside the great gate) and open the Heikhal gate from inside (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 4:6).
in the clearing of the inner altar. Above 3:4.
in the clearing of the menorah. Ibid. halakhah 12.

this one in the Heikhal trims five lamps. For the lighting of the menorah was done in two actions: first they light five lamps, and afterward they light the two remaining lamps (see above 3:16 and below halakhah 4).
they flay and cut up. The manner of flaying and cutting up is explained in Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 6:5.
and of the additional offerings. The limbs of the burnt offerings of the Shabbat and festival additional offerings.

between corner and corner, in the place where the priests walk. On the outer cubit of the altar's roof were the corners; in the cubit adjacent to them there were no fire piles, and this cubit was designated for the priests walking on the altar's roof (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 2:7).
to publicize that it is Rosh Chodesh. Since Rosh Chodesh was determined by the court, it was necessary to publicize that they had sanctified the month.
and they salt the limbs there. As all sacrifices are salted (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:11).
and they scatter. Sprinkle.
when they go with the wood to the pile, etc.. But in carrying the limbs, which is considered a service, they do not scatter.
they blessed one blessing. From the blessings of the Shema.

and the Ten Commandments. In the Temple they read the Ten Commandments every day before the Shema because they are the foundation and beginning of the commandments. Outside the Temple they are not read, so that the heretics will not say that only the Ten Commandments were given to Moses at Sinai (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tamid 5:1).
the third and fourth lotteries. Above 4:7-8.

and afterward the one who merited the clearing of the menorah enters and trims the two lamps. After lighting the first five lamps (above halakhah 3), the one who clears leaves the Heikhal, and afterward he returns to light the two remaining lamps (above 3:16).
and stands on the steps of the Ulam. The steps descending from the Ulam to the courtyard.

the magrefah. A special vessel used for this throwing (Tosafot Yom Tov and Tiferet Yisrael, Tamid 5:6), and some explain that it is a musical instrument and accordingly 'threw it' means he produced many sounds from it (Raavad, Tamid 3:8).

that his brother priests are entering to prostrate and he runs and comes. Each day after the completion of the service in the Heikhal, the priests would enter the Heikhal to prostrate (Tiferet Yisrael, Tamid 7:1).
knows that his brother Levites are entering to speak with song. They gather and prepare to sing at the time of the wine libation of the offering (below halakhah 7).
and the head of the Ma'amad. The officer over the men of the Ma'amad, Israelites who stood each week as representatives of all Israel over the communal offerings (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 6:1).

would station the impure at the east gate because of suspicion, etc.. Those lacking atonement (such as metzora'im) who had immersed and not yet brought their offering stood at the Nicanor Gate at the eastern entrance of the courtyard, so that it would be seen that they had not yet brought the offering and are forbidden to enter the courtyard (and in the Commentary on the Mishnah, Tamid 5:6 he wrote that the metzora'im stood there in order to be ready for the sprinkling of the blood of the guilt offering; and see Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 4:2).

the Priestly Blessing as one blessing, with the Explicit Name, as we explained in its place. They say the three verses of the Priestly Blessing in sequence, without answering amen between verses, and pronounce the Name of God as written and not as it is usually pronounced (Hilchot Tefillah 14:9-10).
they bring up the fine flour of the libations. They burn on the altar fire the meal offering of libations of the tamid offering.
and after the fine flour he burns the chavitin. The High Priest's chavitin.
they bring up the wine for libation. They pour the libation wine into the shittin on the altar.
the Levites say the song. The Levites stand on the platform and sing with their mouths, and together with them others stand and play musical instruments (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 3:3).
with the kinds of music in the Temple. Various musical instruments (see ibid. halakhah 4).
they stand on the table of the fats. The marble table west of the ramp on which they placed the limbs of the offerings (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 2:15).
and the segan. The deputy of the priests, the High Priest's second.
stands at the corner of the altar. At the corner of the altar, to signal to the priests when the libation will begin.
the one appointed over the cymbal. The one in charge of the instrument players (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 7:7).
the cymbal. Cymbals.
they reached the section, etc.. The Levites' song was divided into three parts, and at each part they blew three times.
as we have explained. Above halakhah 5, Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 7:5.
they say song only, etc.. See also Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 3:2.
communal burnt offering... mentioned in the Torah. Tamidim and additional offerings.
and the sacrifices of their peace offerings. The lambs of Atzeret (below 8:1).

a voluntary burnt offering offered from the surplus of the chamber's donation. Voluntary offerings that the community offered from the half-shekel funds left over after they were used to buy the communal offerings of that year (see Hilchot Shekalim 4:9).
libations that come on their own. When the libations were not poured together with the offering but later.
the song Ha'azinu. Deuteronomy 32:1-43.
and they divide it into six sections, etc.. They do not say the whole song on one Shabbat, but each Shabbat they say one section.
Ha-zi-yo la-kh. The acronym for the breaks between the passages.
in the way that they read them in the synagogue. When reading Parashat Ha'azinu on Shabbat in the synagogue they pause at these places (and they are detailed in Hilchot Tefillah 13:5).
at the Shabbat Minchah. At the afternoon tamid.
they say 'Then Moses sang' and 'Who is like You'. Every Shabbat, the two sections (Lechem Mishneh, Mereh HaKorban, Marcheshet Mishneh; and see Rikuv).

at the additional offering of Rosh Hashanah, etc.. The songs of the tamid on all the days of the festivals were the songs of weekdays (see Aruch HaShulchan 114:14), and for the additional offering there were special psalms (for the details of the additional-offering songs of Sukkot see below 10:11; the additional-offering songs of the other festivals and Rosh Chodesh are not mentioned in the Talmud and Rambam, and see Massekhet Soferim chapter 18).

and if it falls on Thursday, they say 'I removed his shoulder from the burden'. Since every Thursday they say 'Sing joyfully' at the tamid offering, in order not to repeat the psalm twice they said 'I removed' at the additional offering (Likkutei Halakhot, end of Tamid, in the view of Rambam).
the song of Rosh Chodesh overrides the song of Shabbat, etc.. Unlike a Yom Tov that falls on Shabbat, when only the Shabbat song is said and not the Yom Tov song (see below 10:11).
and in the order they do every day in the morning, so they do in the afternoon, except, etc.. All the services mentioned for the morning were also done in the afternoon.
for these things are done only every day in the morning, as we have explained. Above 2:2, 2:10-11, 4:8.
like the procedure of the tamid. Above 1:10.
like the procedure of the sin offering that is eaten, which we explained. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot chapter 7.
and it is a communal meal offering as we explained. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 12:3.
and its time is fixed, and therefore it overrides Shabbat and impurity. Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 4:9.

from the Land of Israel, as it is stated, 'and you shall bring the omer of the first of your harvest to the priest'. And at the beginning of the verse it says: 'When you come to the land' (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 8:1).

its mitzvah is to bring from the nearby. According to the rule 'we do not pass over mitzvot': when there is an opportunity to perform a mitzvah with nearby grain, one does not leave it and bring from afar (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 10:2).
ripened early. Ripened.

its mitzvah is to be harvested at night. Learned from the verse 'from when the sickle begins on the standing grain you shall begin to count' (Deuteronomy 16:9), that just as the counting of the omer is at night (see below halakhah 22), so too the harvesting is at night.
the standing grain. Grain that has not been harvested.
the sheaves. Grain that was harvested and bound in bundles.
the fresh. Fresh barley kernels.
the fields in the south. Fields drenched in sun.

he would plow half the field and sow half of it, etc.. Each year he would sow only half the field and plow the other half without sowing, and in this way the grain grew in better quality (see also Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 7:4).
this omer came from barley. Unlike most meal offerings, which came from wheat (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 12:2).
bundles while still attached to the ground. They bind the stalks of barley while still attached.
so that it be harvested with great activity. With publicity and bustle.
three se'ah. About twenty-five liters. Each man harvests one se'ah with his own sickle into a basket.
with three men, three baskets and three sickles. So that the harvest would be finished quickly (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 10:1), and to publicize the matter (Bavli Menachot 64a).
baskets. Baskets.
once it grew dark. The night of the sixteenth of Nisan.
the sun has set. It set.
these are the erring ones who left the community of Israel in the Second Temple period. The Boethusians, who do not believe in the Oral Torah (Mishnah Menachot 10:3).
Shabbat Bereishit. The seventh day of every week since the creation of the world.
for it is only the Shabbat of Yom Tov. And the verse calls the first Yom Tov of Pesach 'Shabbat.'

'and you shall not eat bread or parched grain or fresh ears until this very day'. From here a Torah prohibition is learned against eating from the new grain until the day the omer is offered (for the details of this law see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 10:2-5).

'and they ate of the produce of the land on the day after the Pesach, matzot and parched grain'. The Israelites ate of the new grain when they entered the Land of Israel from the wilderness on the sixteenth of Nisan, which is the day after Pesach, from which it follows that the time of offering the omer and the permission of the new grain depends on Pesach and not on Shabbat.

and if you say that that Pesach, etc.. One could argue against this proof that Pesach that year fell on Shabbat, but in other years they would offer the omer and eat the new grain on the day after Shabbat Bereishit.

how did the verse make the permission to eat depend, etc.. The verse explains that because that day was the day after Pesach they ate, so this is what caused the permission, and it cannot be interpreted as having happened only in that case.
and they beat it. To extract the kernels from the stalks.
and they winnow. They throw it in the wind to separate the husks from the kernels.
and they sort. They complete the separation of the kernels from the waste.
and they roast them on the fire in a perforated tube. They parch the barley kernels in a perforated vessel special for parching kernels, so that the fire reaches all the kernels.
they spread it in the courtyard and the wind blows on it. To cool the kernels from the heat of parching and dry them.
to a mill of coarse grinding. A mill for coarse grinding.

and they take out of it all an isaron sifted through thirteen sieves. They sift the ground barley thirteen times through various sieves until clean fine flour comes out of it, and from it they take an isaron for the meal offering (and see below 8:4-5).
and the rest is redeemed and eaten by anyone. What remains of the barley is redeemed with money, and after its redemption it is non-sacred and anyone may eat it.

and it is liable to challah and exempt from the tithes, as we explained. Something that was in the Temple's possession at the time it became liable for tithes is exempt from tithes even after its redemption (Hilchot Ma'aser 3:25), and it is liable to separation of challah (Hilchot Bikkurim 6:3).
and they mix it with a log of oil... and put a handful of frankincense on it like other meal offerings. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 12:7, 12:9.
and he waves it in the east. Everything requiring waving is waved in the east of the courtyard (ibid. 9:6, and see Piskei u-Shitot there).
and brings it near opposite the point of the southwest corner, like other meal offerings. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 12:6.

and the burnt-offering lamb before the afternoon tamid. The burnt-offering lamb that came with the omer was offered after the offering of the omer (below 9:9), and it was offered near the afternoon tamid. Some punctuate: 'after they offer the additional offering of the day and the burnt-offering lamb...' and explain that the burnt-offering lamb was offered before the omer (Kiryat Sefer, and see the commentary below there).
from the five kinds of grain. Wheat, barley, spelt, oats and rye.
but a beit shelahin in the valleys, etc.. A field thirsty for water, not satisfied with rainwater, and wheat grown in it is disqualified for meal offerings (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 6:12).
but he may not pile up. He may not heap up the grain.
grain that took root. Sent roots into the ground.
before the omer. Before the harvest of the omer (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 10:6).
in the way that it is forbidden to eat it. Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 10:4.
that had not brought forth a third, etc.. When it has not yet grown to a third of its full growth it is considered fodder and not grain, and it is permitted to harvest it for animals.
and they harvest because of the plantings, that they not be ruined. So that the grain not destroy the trees.
he should not make them into bundles. Large bundles of grain made of several tzevatim.
he should leave them as tzevatim. He binds the grain in small bundles and leaves it so (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 10:9).
we have already explained that one does not bring, etc.. Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:9-10.
nor bikkurim. Wheat and barley brought as first fruits (Likkutei Halakhot, Menachot 68b).
the Two Loaves. On Shavuot (below 8:1).
and anyone who offers a meal offering from the new grain first. One who offers a meal offering for the first time from the new grain.

grain that he sowed after the omer was offered and harvested after the omer of the following year was offered. In such a way that the bringing of the Two Loaves and the omer passed over it, but not in the usual order, in which the omer comes first and afterward the Two Loaves, but with the Two Loaves first.

grain that was in the ground and had formed kernels, or whose leaves sprouted when they brought the Two Loaves. And in a way that it had not taken root, for example if he buried stalks in the ground and they put out leaves (chanatah) and only after the bringing of the Two Loaves did they take root (Even HaAzel).
and the harvest is valid. For eating after the offering of the omer, and for meal offerings after the bringing of the Two Loaves (Rikuv).
to count seven complete weeks. To count the days each day for seven weeks.
the days with the weeks. To state how many days have passed and how many weeks have passed.
as it is stated, 'you shall count fifty days'. In addition to what is said, 'and you shall count... seven complete weeks.'
this mitzvah applies to every man of Israel. Unlike the counting of the years of the Jubilee, which falls only on the court (Hilchot Shemitah ve-Yovel 10:1).

and women and slaves are exempt from counting the omer. Women are exempt from positive commandments that are time-bound (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 12:3), and slaves are exempt from positive commandments that women are not obligated in (Hilchot Chagigah 2:1).
the offerings mentioned in the Book of Numbers. Numbers 28:27-30.
a new meal offering, the Two Loaves. Two loaves of leavened bread from the new grain, and their bringing permits the offering of meal offerings from the new grain (above 7:17).
the offerings mentioned in the Book of Leviticus. 23:18-19.
if they did not find new, they bring from the attic. From old grain (already in storage).

wheat that came down with the clouds. That came down with the rain or the wind from the clouds (and the discussion is of wheat that grew in the ground or came down by a miracle, see Rashi and Tosafot, Menachot 69b).
from your dwellings. The Land of Israel.
there is a doubt whether I read of them 'from your dwellings'. They are not from outside the Land, but also not from the Land of Israel.
three se'ah of new wheat... and they sift from them two isaronim. From about twenty-five liters of wheat they produced about five liters of fine flour.
and they rub them and tread on them, etc.. See above 5:6.
and the rest is redeemed and eaten by anyone, etc.. See above 7:12.
the Two Loaves, which are from the new, etc.. Moist grain yields less fine flour than old grain, and barley yields less fine flour than wheat.
and the showbread... is satisfied with eleven sieves. Above 5:6.
the omer... from three se'ah and with thirteen sieves. Above 7:12.
and their kneading and shaping outside. See above 5:7.
as it is stated, 'it alone shall be done for you'. From this verse is learned the permission to do food preparation on Yom Tov for the benefit of an Israelite only (see Hilchot Yom Tov 1:13).
and it is explicit in the Torah that they are leavened. Unlike other meal offerings, which must be matzah, regarding the Two Loaves it is said 'they shall be baked leavened' (Leviticus 23:17).
and how does he do it?. In what manner does he leaven the bread (see also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 9:18 regarding leavening the loaves of the thanksgiving offering).
sourdough. A sour dough of water and flour used to make other dough rise.
into the isaron. Into the vessel in which the isaron is measured.
how is the waving of the bread done with the two peace-offering lambs, etc.. He would wave the two lambs alive with the two loaves beside them together (Lechem Mishneh, Mereh HaKorban).
breast and thigh. The breast and the right hind leg, the parts of an individual's peace offering that are given to the priests.
in the east, in the place of all the wavings. See also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 9:6.
the High Priest takes one of them. See above 4:14.
and the second is divided among all the watches. The festival offerings are divided among all the watches and not only the watch serving that week (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:5).

and both are eaten that entire day and half the night like the flesh of most holy offerings. For communal peace offerings are considered most holy offerings (see Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 1:17), and therefore, unlike an individual's peace offerings, they are eaten only by male priests and only for a day and a night (see also ibid. 9:4, 10:3).
he draws two of them and waves them. And thereby they are sanctified for the loaves of Atzeret.

and the rest are redeemed inside and eaten outside like other non-sacred food. The additional loaves must be redeemed from their sanctity of value, and then they become non-sacred and may be taken out of the courtyard and anyone can eat them (for a similar law regarding loaves of the thanksgiving offering see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 12:15).

he draws two of them and sprinkles their blood not for their sake, etc.. He sprinkles the blood of the first two lambs not for the sake of the lambs of Atzeret, and these offerings are valid but do not fulfill the obligation (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 15:1).

and he waves the two remaining valid ones with the Two Loaves. But if he sprinkles the blood of the first two for their sake, the two remaining ones that became superfluous will be disqualified (Bavli Menachot 48a).
the two loaves hold each other back, and the two lambs hold each other back. One does not fulfill the obligation with one without the other.
if he slaughtered one for its sake. And slaughtered the second not for its sake.
the Two Loaves hold back the lambs. They do not offer the lambs without the bread.
and the two lambs do not hold back the bread. And when there are no lambs, one fulfills the obligation of the bread without lambs.
if the bread was lost, the lambs are lost. They take them out to the burning place.
and their form passes and they go out to the burning place. They do not eat them but wait until they spoil, and then burn them.
and they will bring bread without lambs. So that they would err and think lambs are not needed, even ideally.
that come on this day on account of the bread. Additional to the additional offerings (above halakhah 1).

the ram of the day's additional offering and the two rams that come on account of the bread do not hold each other back. But the two rams that come on account of the bread do hold each other back (Rikuv, Kesef Mishneh, based on Bavli Menachot 45a).
and if they were all slaughtered, they hold each other back. For example, if the blood of one of them was spilled before sprinkling, all were disqualified.
the tamidim do not hold back the additional offerings, etc.. And even the tamidim themselves do not hold each other back (above 1:12).

nor do the additional offerings hold each other back. When there are two additional offerings on the same day (such as Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh), one additional offering does not hold back the other. Likewise the kinds of the additional offering (bulls, rams and lambs) do not hold each other back.
nor does the number of the burnt offerings hold back. The number of animals that must be offered as a burnt offering from one kind (such as two bulls, seven lambs).
if they found only six lambs. On a day when seven lambs must be offered for the additional offering.
only two lambs were found. In addition to that day's tamidim.

the matter is balanced. On one hand the tamidim are more frequent than the additional offerings, and on the other hand the day's additional offerings are more sacred than tomorrow's tamidim (because of the sanctity of the day or because they are already fit to be offered, see Bavli Menachot 49a), and in a conflict between the more frequent and the more sacred there is no preference for either (see below 9:2).
on the first of Tishrei. Rosh Hashanah, which is also Rosh Chodesh Tishrei.
and anything more sacred than its fellow precedes its fellow. Explained below from halakhah 5 onward.

this one stirs the blood until he sprinkles the blood of the more frequent or the blood of the more sacred. The priest who received the blood of the offering that should be second stirs its blood (so that it not congeal) until after the first is offered, and then they offer the blood of the second.
for the blood of the sin offering atones. The sprinkling of the blood atones for the sin for which the sin offering was brought.
because the burnt offering is entirely for the fires. And from a sin offering (and the other offerings) only the emurim are placed on the altar fire.

the blood of a burnt offering and the blood of a guilt offering. The blood of a guilt offering also atones, but it is less sacred than the sin offering (below halakhah 8), and therefore its law is balanced with the blood of the burnt offering.

a sin offering precedes a burnt offering. If he has not yet slaughtered, he slaughters and offers the sin offering and then slaughters the burnt offering. But if he slaughtered the second before finishing the act of the first, he will give the blood of the sin offering before the blood of the burnt offering and burn the limbs of the burnt offering before the emurim of the sin offering, as explained above, halakhah 5 (Rikuv).

as it is stated, 'that which is for the sin offering first'. It is said regarding one obligated in an ascending-and-descending offering who cannot afford an animal, who brings two birds for his sin, one for a burnt offering and one for a sin offering.
a binyan av. A halakhic source that forms the basis for other laws learned from it.
and likewise at the time of setting aside. When he consecrates them for the offering he consecrates the sin offering first.
in the inadvertent error of the community regarding idolatry. When the Sanhedrin erroneously ruled that it is permitted to worship idols and most of the community acted accordingly.
for they bring a bull as a burnt offering and a goat as a sin offering. See Hilchot Shegagot 12:1.
according to the ordinance. From which it follows that one must offer the sacrifices in the order written in the Torah, as explained at the end of the halakhah.
and the bull of the anointed priest. A bull sin offering brought by the High Priest when he erroneously ruled to permit a prohibition punishable by karet and acted on his own ruling (ibid. 15:1).

precedes the bull of communal matter-hidden. A bull sin offering brought by the community when the Sanhedrin erroneously ruled to permit a prohibition punishable by karet and most of the community acted on their ruling (ibid. 12:1).

for such is the order written in the Torah. In the Torah (Numbers 15:24) a bull as a burnt offering is mentioned first, and afterward a goat as a sin offering (see Har HaMoriah, and see Marcheshet Mishneh, who explained differently).
the goat of the nasi. The sin offering goat brought by the king (ibid. 1:4; unlike the rest of the people, who bring a female lamb or female goat for their sin offering).
and the individual's she-goat precedes the lamb, etc.. An individual who sinned in idolatry brings specifically a she-goat, and for other sins brings a she-goat or a lamb (ibid.).

even the bird sin offering of a woman after childbirth precedes her lamb. A woman after childbirth brings a bird as a sin offering, and a lamb or a bird as a burnt offering (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:3). Her sin offering precedes her burnt offering even when the burnt offering is from an animal (as explained above, halakhah 6, even though this sin offering lacks the distinction of a sin offering, since it does not atone for a particular sin).

for its blood is placed on four horns and on the base. See Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:7. Whereas the blood of a guilt offering is thrown in two applications that are four on the lower part of the altar (ibid. halakhah 6).

except for the guilt offering of the metzora, because it comes by way of preparation. For the sake of preparing and purifying the metzora. The metzora who has been purified brings three offerings: a sin offering, a burnt offering and a guilt offering (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:3), and the completion of his purification process depends on offering the guilt offering and sprinkling its blood on the metzora, and therefore it is more important than the sin offering and precedes it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Zevachim 10:5, and see Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 5:3).
the guilt offering precedes the thanksgiving offering and the nazirite's ram because it is most holy. And they are lesser sacrifices (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 1:17).
because they are eaten for one day and require bread. And peace offerings are eaten for two days and a night (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:6-7).

and the thanksgiving offering precedes the nazirite's ram because it has four kinds of meal offering. With the thanksgiving offering one brings forty loaves of four kinds (ibid. 9:17-18), and with the nazirite's ram one brings twenty loaves of two kinds (ibid. halakhah 23).
peace offerings precede the firstborn because they require two applications that are four. And the firstborn requires one pouring opposite the base (ibid. 5:17).
and they require semichah. Ibid. 3:6.
and waving. Ibid. 9:6.
and libations. Ibid. 2:2.

the firstborn precedes animal tithe because its sanctity is from the womb and it is eaten by priests only. But the tithe must be consecrated (see Hilchot Bechorot 7:1) and it is eaten by the owners (ibid. 6:4).

because it is a zevach and has in it most holy parts, its blood and its emurim. The tithe precedes a bird because it is a species of animal. And although birds are most holy and the tithe is a lesser sacrifice, the tithe also has an aspect of most holy, since its blood and emurim that go up to the altar are considered most holy (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Zevachim 10:3).
and the bird sin offering precedes an animal burnt offering. Above, halakhah 6.
for they have been increased in libations. Their libations of fine flour and wine are greater (for the measure of libations see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 2:4).
for among the emurim of lambs is the fat tail. In addition to the other emurim, the fat tail of the lamb is burned (ibid. 1:18).

the omer precedes the lamb that comes with it. They offer it first. Some explained that if he can bring only one of them, he brings the omer and not the lamb (Minchat Chinuch, mitzvah 307, in the view of Kiryat Sefer, and see above 7:12).

and the Two Loaves precede the two lambs. So that if it is impossible to bring both, he brings the bread and not the lambs (Minchat Chinuch there, and see above 8:15). Some explained that they bring them to the courtyard first (Chiddushei HaDrash, Horayot 2:4), or that they are occupied with preparing them first (Rash Shirkin, Horayot 13a).
an item that comes on account of the day. The omer on the sixteenth of Nisan and the Two Loaves on Shavuot.
precedes an item that comes on account of the bread. The lamb that comes with the omer and the two lambs that come with the Two Loaves.

the meal offering of a man precedes the meal offering of a woman. When the two meal offerings are equal (Har HaMoriah, based on Yerushalmi Horayot 3:4). And the same is true of all other offerings (Radbaz).
the meal offering of a sinner precedes a voluntary meal offering because it comes for a sin. Its offering atones for the sin (see also above halakhah 5).

a voluntary meal offering and the meal offering of a sotah, whichever of them he wishes he may put first. The voluntary meal offering is preferable because it is of wheat and has oil and frankincense, and the sotah's meal offering is preferable because it comes to clarify a sin (Bavli Zevachim 90a). Therefore he may put first whichever meal offering he wishes.

and wine precedes oil, etc.. One may volunteer all of these for the altar: wine is poured on the altar, and oil, frankincense and wood are burned (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:1), and one can also donate salt for salting the offerings. And if one volunteered a meal offering and another volunteered wine, they attend first to the one who brought the meal offering, and so with the other examples (Chiddushei HaDrash, Zevachim 10:2).
and peace offerings of the day. That were slaughtered today.
those of last night precede, for their time has come. The time for eating them ends earlier.

peace offerings of last night and a sin offering or guilt offering of the day, etc.. Although the time for eating the peace offerings will end at the end of the day (for they are eaten on the day of slaughter and the next day until evening), while the time for eating the sin offering and guilt offering lasts until midnight, their eating takes precedence.
as we have explained. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 1:17.
and this ram is called the people's ram. Because it was brought from the community, and in addition the High Priest would bring another ram as a burnt offering (Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 1:1).
and it is eaten in the evening. At the end of the fast.
and the community also offers a sin offering goat and it is burned, etc.. And in addition the High Priest would bring another bull as a sin offering of his own (ibid.).

and this is an additional offering on its own. Although Shemini Atzeret is adjacent to Sukkot, it is not considered an additional day of Sukkot but an independent Yom Tov, and the number of its offerings does not correspond to the additional offerings of Sukkot (and see also below halakhah 13 regarding the division of work among the watches).
he would pour the water by itself. He would pour the water on its own without mixing it with the wine.
and poured both from one vessel. When they are mixed.
for the zevach. For the tamid offering.
and at the southwest corner he would pour upward. See also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:10.
and everything goes down to the shittin as we explained. The water would go down from above into the openings in the base (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 2:1).
a flask. A jug.
the Siloam. The Siloam spring located south of the Temple Mount.
they reached the Water Gate. Of the southern gates of the courtyard (see the shape of the courtyard in Hilchot Beit HaBechirah, end of chapter 5).
they blew a tekiah, a teruah, and a tekiah. See also Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 7:6.

and turned to his left. Since the libation was at the southwest corner, to the left of the ramp (which was on the south side of the altar), the one ascending to pour (unlike others ascending the altar) would turn at the top of the ramp to the left (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:11).
and they were perforated like two thin nostrils. At the bottom of the bowls were protrusions with holes for the wine and water to flow out.

and the water one had a thinner hole than the wine one. In both libations he poured three logs, and so that the libation would end at once, the hole of the water (which flows out faster) was smaller than that of the wine.
raise your hand. So that everyone could see that he is pouring into the bowls.

for they said it was a heretic who says that water is not poured. Since the water libation is not explicit in the Torah but is a law given to Moses at Sinai (above halakhah 6), the heretics who deny the Oral Torah thought that water should not be poured.
and it is not one of the service vessels. So that they not think this water is sanctified for sanctifying hands and feet and use it for that (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sukkah 4:9).

was uncovered. The cover of the barrel was removed, and a drink that was in an uncovered vessel, for which there is concern that a snake may have injected venom into it, is disqualified for the altar (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 6:10).

on each and every day of the festival they would say a song on its own for the day's additional offering. At the wine libation of the additional offering they would say a song (above 6:8-9). On Sukkot they would say each day a special song for that day.

and if Shabbat falls on one of them, it is moved, it is postponed. And if Shabbat falls on one of the days of Chol HaMoed, at the additional offering of that day they sing the song of Shabbat (see above 6:10 in Piskei u-Shitot), and after Shabbat they continue the order of the songs from where they left off, so that the psalm of Friday of Chol HaMoed is postponed and not said.
we have already explained that all the priestly watches are twenty-four and all of them work equally on the festivals. Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:3-6.
and whoever offered the bull today would not offer a bull tomorrow. So that all the watches would offer bulls.

and on the eighth they all cast lots again as one, like the other festivals. For the offerings of Shemini Atzeret do not belong to the offerings of Sukkot (above halakhah 5), and therefore they did not take into account the division of work of the days of Sukkot, but conducted a new lottery among the watches.
as we have explained. That all the watches are equal on the festivals (above halakhah 12, Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:4).

there was the meal offering of the libations of the additional offerings and the tamidim, sixty-one isaron. For all the burnt offerings offered on this day: the tamidim, the Shabbat additional offering and the festival additional offering.

and one never mixes libations, etc.. They do not mix the fine flour and wine of the libations of offerings of different kinds. But of the same kind they mix (Marcheshet Mishneh, and see below halakhah 17 onward).
meal offerings of libations. Of different kinds (lambs, rams, bulls).

after each kind was mixed on its own they are valid. And if they were mixed before kneading: if the meal offerings of bulls and rams were mixed, the meal offerings are valid, and if the meal offerings of bulls or rams were mixed with the meal offerings of lambs, the meal offerings are invalid (for in the meal offering of lambs the ratio of fine flour to oil is three logs to an isaron, whereas in the meal offerings of bulls and rams the ratio is two logs to an isaron; Marcheshet Mishneh, Likkutei Halakhot, Menachot 89b). And all this is for meal offerings of different kinds, but meal offerings of the same kind may be mixed even ideally (above halakhah 15).

and once the meal offerings were kneaded... it is permitted to mix their wine ideally. When the meal offerings are separate it is forbidden ideally to mix their wine, lest he mix the fine flour (Bavli Menachot 89b). And after the meal offerings were mixed or burned, it is permitted to mix only the wine of bulls with the wine of rams (whose fine flour, even if mixed before kneading, is not disqualified), but not the wine of bulls or rams with that of lambs (below halakhah 19).
libation wine of last night. For it is permitted to bring the libation meal offering even several days after the offering of the sacrifice (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 2:12).

with the libation wine of lambs. He mixes libation wine of lambs with libation wine of lambs (see Rikuv and Kesef Mishneh, who emended it: 'libation wine of lambs with libation wine of lambs,' but even without the emendation the halakhah is interpreted this way and the language is merely brief; and so it is in Mishnah Menachot 9:4 according to Rambam's text).
but they do not mix libation wine of lambs with libation wine of bulls and rams. Even after their meal offerings were offered or mixed.

and one never mixes wine ideally, etc.. The wine of bulls with the wine of rams (and likewise lamb wine of last night or of an individual with lamb wine of today or of the community - Rikuv). But the wine of different offerings of the same kind they mix even ideally (see above halakhah 15).
as we have explained. Above halakhah 18.
